STEP 1: Add all W-2 wages (Box 1)
STEP 2: Add all tips (reported and unreported)
STEP 3: Add net profit from Schedule C
STEP 4: Add net profit from Schedule F
STEP 5: Add union strike benefits
STEP 6: Add long-term disability (if before retirement age)
STEP 7: Add nontaxable combat pay (if you elect to include it)
STEP 8: Subtract 1/2 of self-employment tax

= TOTAL EARNED INCOME FOR EITC

EXAMPLES OF EARNED INCOME CALCULATIONS

EXAMPLE 1: W-2 Employee
- W-2 wages: $28,000
- Tips (unreported): $2,000
- **Total earned income: $30,000**

EXAMPLE 2: Self-Employed
- Gross business income: $50,000
- Business expenses: $18,000
- Net profit: $32,000
- Self-employment tax: $4,521
- Half of SE tax: $2,261
- **Earned income: $29,739** ($32,000 - $2,261)

EXAMPLE 3: Multiple Jobs
- W-2 Job 1: $15,000
- W-2 Job 2: $8,000
- Side business net profit: $5,000
- SE tax on side business: $707
- Half of SE tax: $354
- **Earned income: $27,646** (15,000 + 8,000 + 5,000 - 354)

EXAMPLE 4: Military with Combat Pay
- Regular military pay (taxable): $35,000
- Combat pay (nontaxable): $10,000
- Elect to include combat pay: Yes
- **Earned income: $45,000**

IMPORTANT DISTINCTIONS

EARNED INCOME vs. ADJUSTED GROSS INCOME (AGI):
- **Earned income:** Only from work
- **AGI:** All income minus certain deductions
- **EITC uses the LESSER of earned income OR AGI**

EARNED INCOME vs. TAXABLE INCOME:
- **Earned income:** Specific types from work
- **Taxable income:** AGI minus standard or itemized deductions
- **EITC based on earned income, not taxable income**

EARNED INCOME vs. GROSS INCOME:
- **Earned income:** Only work-related compensation
- **Gross income:** All income from all sources
- **Earned income is a subset of gross income**

WHERE TO REPORT EARNED INCOME

ON YOUR TAX RETURN:
- Form 1040, line 1: Wages, salaries, tips
- Schedule C: Business income
- Schedule F: Farm income  
- Schedule EIC: If claiming with children

THE IRS WILL VERIFY:
- W-2s and 1099s are matched to your return
- Self-employment income against bank deposits
- All sources of income

WHY IT MATTERS

EITC ELIGIBILITY:
- Must have earned income to qualify
- Amount of credit based on earned income
- Too little earned income = no credit
- Too much earned income = no credit
- There's a "sweet spot" for maximum credit

STRATEGY:
- Understand what counts as earned income
- Report all earned income (IRS will find it anyway)
- Don't confuse earned income with other income types
- Calculate correctly to maximize EITC

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID

❌ Counting Social Security as earned income
❌ Counting unemployment as earned income
❌ Forgetting to subtract 1/2 SE tax
❌ Not reporting cash income
❌ Including investment income as earned income
❌ Confusing earned income with AGI
❌ Not electing to include combat pay when beneficial

✓ Only count income from work
✓ Include ALL W-2 wages
✓ Calculate self-employment income correctly
✓ Report tips (even unreported ones)
✓ Consider combat pay election
✓ Subtract 1/2 of SE tax
✓ Keep good records

SUMMARY CHECKLIST

EARNED INCOME FOR EITC:
☑ W-2 wages, salaries, tips
☑ Net self-employment income (minus 1/2 SE tax)
☑ Union strike benefits
☑ Long-term disability (before retirement age)
☑ Nontaxable combat pay (if elected)

NOT EARNED INCOME:
☐ Social Security benefits
☐ Unemployment compensation
☐ Pensions and annuities
☐ Investment income
☐ Welfare benefits
☐ Alimony and child support
☐ Most nontaxable income

For detailed information on specific types of income, consult:
- IRS Publication 596 (Earned Income Credit)
- IRS Publication 525 (Taxable and Nontaxable Income)
- IRS.gov EITC resources

Source: IRS.gov - Earned Income and EITC Tables
Last Updated: 2024
Informational only, not tax advice.

title: Irs Official Who Qualifies
content:
IRS Official Guide: Who Qualifies for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
Source: IRS.gov Official Website

BASIC QUALIFYING RULES

To qualify for the EITC, you must meet ALL of these requirements:

1. Have EARNED INCOME
Earned income includes wages, salaries, tips, and net self-employment income. See IRS guidance on earned income for complete details.

2. Have INVESTMENT INCOME below the limit
Your investment income must be within the annual limit (check current year limit). Investment income includes interest, dividends, and capital gains.

3. Have a VALID SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER by the due date of your return (including extensions)
The SSN must be valid for employment purposes and issued on or before the tax return due date.

4. Be a U.S. CITIZEN or RESIDENT ALIEN all year
You must maintain this status for the entire tax year.

5. NOT file Form 2555, Foreign Earned Income
If you claim the foreign earned income exclusion, you cannot claim EITC.

6. Meet certain rules if you are separated from your spouse and not filing a joint tax return
Special rules apply for separated spouses.

SPECIAL QUALIFYING RULES

The EITC has special qualifying rules for:
- Military members (including combat pay elections)
- Clergy members (including housing allowances)
- Taxpayers and their relatives with disabilities

If you're unsure if you qualify for the EITC, use the IRS EITC Assistant tool available on IRS.gov.

VALID SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER REQUIREMENTS

To qualify for the EITC, you, your spouse if filing jointly, and any child claimed must have a valid Social Security number (SSN) issued on or before the due date of the tax return (including extensions).

AN SSN IS NOT VALID FOR THE EITC IF:
- It was issued after the due date of your return (including extensions), OR
- It was issued solely to apply for or receive a federally funded benefit (such as Medicaid) and does not authorize you to work

IMPORTANT NOTE ABOUT EMPLOYMENT AUTHORIZATION:
If you, your spouse, or your child has a Social Security card with "Not valid for employment" printed on it and the immigration status has changed to a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, you must ask the Social Security Administration for a Social Security card without the legend.

Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITINs) do NOT qualify for EITC. You must have a valid SSN.

U.S. CITIZEN OR RESIDENT ALIEN REQUIREMENT

To claim the EITC, you must be a U.S. citizen or resident alien for the entire year.

EXCEPTION FOR NONRESIDENT ALIENS:
If you were a nonresident alien for any part of the tax year, you can only claim the EITC if:
- Your filing status is married filing jointly, AND
- Your spouse is a U.S. citizen or resident alien, AND
- You choose to be treated as a U.S. resident

FILING STATUS REQUIREMENTS

Eligible filing statuses to claim EITC:
✓ Married filing jointly
✓ Head of household
✓ Qualifying surviving spouse
✓ Single
✓ Married filing separately (with special rules)

MARRIED FILING SEPARATELY:
Generally, you cannot claim EITC if you file married filing separately. However, there are limited exceptions for taxpayers who are separated from their spouses.

HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD:
To file as head of household, you must:
- Be unmarried or considered unmarried on the last day of the year
- Pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home for the year
- Have a qualifying person live with you for more than half the year

QUALIFYING SURVIVING SPOUSE:
You may qualify as a qualifying surviving spouse if:
- Your spouse died less than 2 years before the tax year you're claiming the EITC
- You did not remarry before the end of that year
- You paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for the year
- You have a child or stepchild you can claim as a relative (this does not include a foster child) and who lived with you the entire year

For more information on filing status, see IRS Publication 501, Dependents, Standard Deductions, and Filing Information, or use the Interactive Tax Assistant on IRS.gov to determine your filing status.

CLAIMING THE EITC WITHOUT A QUALIFYING CHILD

You can claim the EITC without a qualifying child if you meet the EITC basic qualifying rules AND you:

1. Lived in the UNITED STATES for more than half the tax year
   The United States includes:
   - The 50 states
   - The District of Columbia
   - U.S. military bases
   
   The United States does NOT include:
   - U.S. territories such as Guam, the Virgin Islands or Puerto Rico

2. CANNOT be claimed as a qualifying child of another taxpayer or dependent of another person
   - If someone else can claim you as a qualifying child, you cannot claim EITC
   - If someone else claims you as a dependent, you cannot claim EITC

3. Meet the AGE REQUIREMENTS
   - You must be at least age 25 but under age 65 at the end of the year
   - If married and filing a joint return, at least one spouse must meet the age rule
   - Age is determined as of December 31 of the tax year

SUMMARY OF AGE RULES FOR WORKERS WITHOUT QUALIFYING CHILDREN:
Minimum Age: 25 (on December 31)
Maximum Age: 64 (on December 31)
If married filing jointly: At least ONE spouse must meet the age requirement

OTHER TAX CREDITS YOU MAY QUALIFY FOR

If you qualify for the EITC, you may also qualify for these other tax credits:

1. CHILD TAX CREDIT and CREDIT FOR OTHER DEPENDENTS
   - Provides credit for qualifying children and other dependents
   - Different rules than EITC

2. CHILD AND DEPENDENT CARE CREDIT
   - For expenses paid for care of qualifying persons
   - Enables you to work or look for work

3. EDUCATION CREDITS
   - American Opportunity Tax Credit
   - Lifetime Learning Credit
   - For qualified education expenses

Each credit has its own eligibility rules. Use IRS tools and publications to determine if you qualify for multiple credits.

KEY REMINDERS

✓ You must file a tax return to claim the EITC, even if you don't owe any tax
✓ The EITC is refundable - you can get money back even if you owe no tax
✓ Use IRS Free File if your income qualifies
✓ VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) provides free tax help
✓ The IRS EITC Assistant can help you determine eligibility
✓ Keep good records in case of an audit
✓ Refunds may be delayed - by law, the IRS cannot issue EITC refunds before mid-February

COMMON DISQUALIFICATIONS

You CANNOT claim EITC if:
✗ You don't have earned income
✗ Your investment income exceeds the annual limit
✗ You file Form 2555 (Foreign Earned Income)
✗ You don't have a valid SSN for everyone on the return
✗ You file as Married Filing Separately (except in limited circumstances)
✗ You are a nonresident alien (unless meeting the exception)
✗ You don't meet the age requirements (if claiming without a child)
✗ Someone else can claim you as a dependent (if claiming without a child)

WHERE TO GET HELP

IRS Resources:
- EITC Assistant tool on IRS.gov
- Publication 596: Earned Income Credit (EIC)
- Publication 501: Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information
- Interactive Tax Assistant for filing status
- IRS Free File (for qualifying taxpayers)
- VITA locations (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance)
- IRS helpline: 1-800-829-1040

Always use official IRS resources or consult with a qualified tax professional for your specific situation.

Source: IRS.gov official website
Publication: Who Qualifies for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
Last Updated: 2024

Disclaimer: This information is for general guidance only. Tax laws are complex and change frequently. Consult IRS Publication 596 or a qualified tax professional for your specific situation. Informational only, not tax advice.

title: Eitc Credit Amounts 2024
content:
EITC Credit Amounts and Phase-Out Information for Tax Year 2024

Maximum Credit Amounts by Number of Qualifying Children

For Tax Year 2024, the maximum EITC amounts are:
- No qualifying children: $632
- One qualifying child: $4,213
- Two qualifying children: $6,960
- Three or more qualifying children: $7,830

These amounts are the MAXIMUM you can receive. Your actual credit depends on your earned income and filing status.

Income Limits for Tax Year 2024

SINGLE, HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD, OR QUALIFYING SURVIVING SPOUSE:
No qualifying children:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $18,591
- Maximum credit: $632

One qualifying child:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $49,084
- Maximum credit: $4,213

Two qualifying children:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $55,768
- Maximum credit: $6,960

Three or more qualifying children:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $59,899
- Maximum credit: $7,830

MARRIED FILING JOINTLY:
No qualifying children:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $24,210
- Maximum credit: $632

One qualifying child:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $55,768
- Maximum credit: $4,213

Two qualifying children:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $62,449
- Maximum credit: $6,960

Three or more qualifying children:
- Maximum earned income/AGI: $66,819
- Maximum credit: $7,830

How the EITC is Calculated

The EITC has three phases:

PHASE 1: Earning Phase (Credit Increases with Income)
- As your earned income increases from $0, your credit increases
- Each dollar of earned income increases your credit by a percentage (called the "credit percentage")
- This continues until you reach the maximum credit amount

PHASE 2: Plateau Phase (Maximum Credit)
- Once you reach a certain income level, you receive the maximum credit
- Your credit remains at this maximum as income increases within a range
- This is the "sweet spot" where you get the full credit

PHASE 3: Phase-Out Range (Credit Decreases)
- After the plateau, the credit begins to decrease as income increases
- For each additional dollar earned, your credit decreases by a percentage (called the "phase-out percentage")
- Eventually, at the maximum income limit, the credit reaches zero

Credit Percentages for Tax Year 2024:

NO QUALIFYING CHILDREN:
- Credit percentage: 7.65%
- Phase-out percentage: 7.65%
- Phase-out begins: $9,800 (Single), $16,370 (Married)

ONE QUALIFYING CHILD:
- Credit percentage: 34%
- Phase-out percentage: 15.98%
- Phase-out begins: $21,560 (Single), $28,120 (Married)

TWO QUALIFYING CHILDREN:
- Credit percentage: 40%
- Phase-out percentage: 21.06%
- Phase-out begins: $21,560 (Single), $28,120 (Married)

THREE OR MORE QUALIFYING CHILDREN:
- Credit percentage: 45%
- Phase-out percentage: 21.06%
- Phase-out begins: $21,560 (Single), $28,120 (Married)

Example Calculations:

EXAMPLE 1: Single with Two Children, Earned Income $25,000
- Income is in the plateau phase
- Qualifies for maximum credit: $6,960

EXAMPLE 2: Single with Two Children, Earned Income $45,000
- Income is in phase-out range
- Credit begins reducing from maximum
- Phase-out amount: ($45,000 - $21,560) × 21.06% = $4,935
- Credit: $6,960 - $4,935 = $2,025

EXAMPLE 3: Married with One Child, Earned Income $18,000
- Income is in earning phase
- Maximum credit would be $4,213
- But at $18,000 income, child must meet all tests
- Credit calculation: $18,000 × 34% = $6,120
- But maximum is $4,213, so credit = $4,213

EXAMPLE 4: Single, No Children, Earned Income $12,000
- Income is in earning phase
- Credit: $12,000 × 7.65% = $918
- But maximum for no children is $632
- Credit = $632 (maximum)

Investment Income Limit

For 2024, you cannot claim the EITC if your investment income is more than $11,000.

Investment income includes:
- Taxable interest
- Tax-exempt interest
- Dividends
- Capital gains
- Royalty income
- Rental income (passive)
- Income from passive activities

Special Rules for Disaster Areas

If you lived in a federally declared disaster area, special rules may apply:
- You may be able to use your prior year's earned income if it was higher
- This can qualify you for a larger credit
- Check IRS disaster relief announcements for specific disasters

Using Prior Year Earned Income

If your 2024 earned income is less than your 2023 earned income, you can elect to use your 2023 earned income to figure your 2024 EITC.

This can help you if:
- You lost a job in 2024
- Your hours were reduced
- You took time off for medical reasons
- Any situation where your 2024 income was lower

To use prior year income:
- You must have had earned income in both years
- Complete the EITC worksheet in the instructions
- Attach a statement to your return electing to use prior year income

EITC and Other Credits

The EITC can be combined with other tax credits:
- Child Tax Credit (CTC)
- Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC)
- Child and Dependent Care Credit
- Education credits (American Opportunity, Lifetime Learning)
- Premium Tax Credit (for health insurance)

These credits don't reduce each other - you can claim all that you qualify for.

EITC Refund Timing

Important dates:
- IRS cannot issue EITC refunds before mid-February (by law)
- This delay applies to the entire refund if you claim EITC
- File early, but expect refund after February 15
- Use IRS "Where's My Refund?" tool to track your refund

State EITC Programs

Many states offer their own EITC that supplements the federal credit:
- Some are refundable, some are non-refundable
- Percentages of federal EITC vary by state
- Some states have separate applications
- Check your state's tax website for details

States with EITC programs (as of 2024):
California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin

Historical Context

The EITC amounts are adjusted annually for inflation. They have generally increased over time:
- 2023 maximum (3+ children): $7,430
- 2024 maximum (3+ children): $7,830
- Increase due to inflation adjustments

Important Reminders

1. You must file a tax return to claim the EITC, even if you don't owe tax
2. The credit is refundable - you can get money back even if you owe no tax
3. Both earned income AND AGI must be within the limits
4. Use the IRS EITC Assistant to estimate your credit
5. Keep good records in case of an audit
6. File electronically for fastest processing
7. Choose direct deposit for fastest refund

Source: IRS Publication 596, IRS Revenue Procedure 2023-34, IRS Form 1040 Instructions

title: Eitc Quick Reference
content:
EITC Quick Reference Guide - Fast Facts and Checklists

Quick Eligibility Checklist

DO YOU QUALIFY FOR EITC? Check ALL that apply:

□ I have earned income (wages, salary, self-employment)
□ My investment income is $11,000 or less
□ I have a valid Social Security Number
□ I am a U.S. citizen or resident alien all year
□ I am NOT filing Form 2555 (Foreign Earned Income)
□ My filing status is NOT "Married Filing Separately"
□ I meet the age requirements (if no qualifying children)
□ My income is under the limit for my situation

If ALL boxes are checked, you likely qualify!

Fast Facts - 2024 Tax Year

Maximum Credits:
• No children: $632
• 1 child: $4,213
• 2 children: $6,960
• 3+ children: $7,830

Income Limits (Single/HOH):
• No children: $18,591
• 1 child: $49,084
• 2 children: $55,768
• 3+ children: $59,899

Income Limits (Married Filing Jointly):
• No children: $24,210
• 1 child: $55,768
• 2 children: $62,449
• 3+ children: $66,819

Investment Income Limit: $11,000

The Four Tests for Qualifying Children

A child must pass ALL four tests:

1. RELATIONSHIP
□ Your son, daughter, stepchild, foster child, sibling, or descendant

2. AGE
□ Under 19, OR
□ Under 24 if full-time student, OR
□ Any age if permanently/totally disabled

3. RESIDENCY
□ Lived with you in the U.S. more than 6 months

4. JOINT RETURN
□ Not filing a joint return (or only to claim refund)

Age Requirements (No Qualifying Children)

□ At least age 25 on December 31
□ Under age 65 on December 31
□ Cannot be claimed as a dependent by someone else

What Counts as Earned Income?

YES - These COUNT:
✓ Wages, salaries, tips
✓ Self-employment net income
✓ Union strike benefits
✓ Long-term disability (before retirement age)
✓ Nontaxable combat pay (if you elect to include it)

NO - These DON'T count:
✗ Interest and dividends
✗ Social Security
✗ Unemployment
✗ Pensions
✗ Alimony
✗ Child support
✗ Welfare benefits

Common Reasons for EITC Denial

TOP REASONS EITC IS DENIED:
1. Child doesn't meet all four tests
2. Missing or invalid Social Security Numbers
3. Income too high
4. Investment income over $11,000
5. Filing status "Married Filing Separately"
6. No earned income
7. Missing Schedule EIC (if required)
8. Child claimed by someone else

Documents to Keep (For 3 Years)

FOR QUALIFYING CHILDREN:
□ Birth certificate
□ School records
□ Medical records
□ Childcare records
□ Any proof of residence

FOR INCOME:
□ W-2 forms
□ 1099 forms
□ Schedule C (if self-employed)
□ Bank statements

FOR FILING STATUS:
□ Marriage certificate or divorce decree
□ Bills showing you paid household costs

Quick Filing Tips

✓ File electronically - fastest processing
✓ Use direct deposit - fastest refund
✓ File early (but refund won't issue until mid-February)
✓ Use IRS EITC Assistant to check eligibility
✓ Complete Schedule EIC if you have qualifying children
✓ Double-check all Social Security Numbers
✓ Keep copies of everything
✓ Respond immediately to any IRS letters

EITC Refund Timing

⏰ Important Dates:
• File anytime after January 1
• IRS cannot issue refunds before mid-February (by law)
• Most refunds arrive within 21 days after February 15
• Use "Where's My Refund?" tool to track

Free Help Available

FREE TAX PREPARATION:
• VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance)
  - For income under $60,000
  - Find locations: irs.gov/vita or call 1-800-906-9887

• TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly)
  - Age 60 and older
  - Find locations: call 1-888-227-7669

• IRS Free File
  - Income under $73,000
  - Online at irs.gov/freefile

PHONE HELP:
• IRS Main Line: 1-800-829-1040
• EITC Hotline: 1-800-829-1040 (mention EITC)
• TTY: 1-800-829-4059

ONLINE TOOLS:
• EITC Assistant: irs.gov/eitc-assistant
• Where's My Refund?: irs.gov/refunds

Red Flags - Don't Do These

🚫 NEVER:
• Claim children who don't qualify
• Make up income amounts
• Use someone else's SSN
• Ignore IRS letters
• Let preparer keep your refund
• File as Head of Household if you don't qualify
• Claim EITC during a ban period

⚠️ WARNING SIGNS of Bad Tax Preparers:
• Promises specific refund before seeing documents
• Charges percentage of refund
• Won't sign your return
• Won't provide their PTIN
• Wants your refund direct deposited to their account

State EITC Quick List

STATES WITH REFUNDABLE EITC:
California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, D.C., Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, Washington (separate program), Wisconsin

Don't forget to claim your state credit!

Special Situations Quick Guide

MILITARY:
• Combat pay can be elected to count
• Overseas assignments don't affect residency test

STUDENTS:
• Being a student doesn't disqualify YOU
• Child under 24 can qualify if full-time student

SELF-EMPLOYED:
• Use Schedule C net profit
• Subtract 1/2 of self-employment tax
• Keep good records!

DIVORCED PARENTS:
• Child must live with you 6+ months for EITC
• Form 8332 doesn't affect EITC
• Custodial parent typically claims EITC

FOSTER CHILDREN:
• Must be placed by authorized agency
• Must live with you 6+ months
• Meets relationship test

Prior Year EITC

□ Missed EITC in prior years?
□ Can file amended return (Form 1040-X)
□ Up to 3 years from original due date
□ Can still get your refund!

Example: In 2024, you can still claim:
• 2023 EITC (until April 15, 2027)
• 2022 EITC (until April 15, 2026)
• 2021 EITC (until April 15, 2025)

Calculation Quick Reference

HOW EITC IS CALCULATED:
1. Determine number of qualifying children (0, 1, 2, or 3+)
2. Calculate earned income
3. Calculate AGI
4. Use LOWER of earned income or AGI
5. Find your phase (earning, plateau, or phase-out)
6. Look up credit amount or use IRS tables
7. Verify investment income under $11,000

FORMULA (Simplified):
• Earning phase: Income × Credit %
• Plateau: Maximum credit
• Phase-out: Max credit - (Excess income × Phase-out %)

One-Minute Eligibility Test

Answer these 5 questions:

1. Do you have earned income (from work)? YES/NO
2. Is your income under the limit? YES/NO
3. Do you have a valid SSN? YES/NO
4. Are you a U.S. citizen/resident alien? YES/NO
5. Is your investment income $11,000 or less? YES/NO

If you answered YES to all 5: You likely qualify for EITC!
Use IRS EITC Assistant to verify and estimate your credit amount.

Important Phone Numbers

• IRS General: 1-800-829-1040
• Identity Theft: 1-800-908-4490
• Taxpayer Advocate: 1-877-777-4778
• VITA Locations: 1-800-906-9887
• TCE Locations: 1-888-227-7669
• IRS TTY: 1-800-829-4059

Key IRS Publications

• Publication 596 - EITC (Main guide)
• Publication 501 - Dependents and Filing Status
• Publication 503 - Child and Dependent Care
• Publication 929 - Tax Rules for Children
• Publication 17 - Your Federal Income Tax

Download free at: irs.gov/forms

What to Do If...

IF YOU GET AN IRS LETTER:
1. Don't panic - read it carefully
2. Note the deadline
3. Gather requested documents
4. Respond by deadline
5. Keep copies of everything
6. Send certified mail

IF YOUR EITC IS DENIED:
1. Read the explanation
2. File Form 8862 if required
3. Correct any errors
4. Provide additional documentation
5. Appeal if you disagree

IF YOU NEED TO AMEND:
1. Use Form 1040-X
2. Explain the changes
3. Attach supporting documents
4. Allow 16-20 weeks for processing

IF YOU CAN'T PAY:
1. File your return on time anyway
2. Request payment plan
3. Contact IRS to discuss options
4. Don't ignore the issue

Checklist for Filing

BEFORE YOU FILE:
□ Gathered all W-2s and 1099s
□ Collected SSNs for everyone
□ Determined filing status
□ Verified qualifying children meet all tests
□ Checked income limits
□ Used EITC Assistant
□ Gathered supporting documents
□ Chose reputable tax preparer or software

WHEN FILING:
□ Completed main return accurately
□ Filled out Schedule EIC (if children)
□ Double-checked all SSNs
□ Reviewed entire return
□ Signed and dated return
□ Kept copies for records
□ Filed electronically
□ Selected direct deposit

AFTER FILING:
□ Kept copy in safe place
□ Noted when to expect refund
□ Checked "Where's My Refund?"
□ Responded to any IRS letters
□ Filed state return
□ Saved documents for 3 years

Remember: EITC is YOUR money - claim it if you qualify!

Source: IRS Publication 596, IRS.gov, EITC Central

title: Eitc Special Situations
content:
EITC Special Situations and Circumstances

Military Personnel and EITC

Nontaxable Combat Pay:
- Military personnel can elect to include nontaxable combat pay as earned income
- This election can increase your EITC
- Combat pay is shown in box 12 of Form W-2 with code Q
- You choose whether to include it - calculate both ways to see which is better

Benefits of Including Combat Pay:
- May increase your EITC
- May help you meet the earned income requirements
- Can make the difference between qualifying or not qualifying

How to Report:
- Enter the amount from box 12 (code Q) on the EITC Worksheet
- Don't include it elsewhere on your tax return (it's nontaxable)
- Make the election on your return

Military Assignments Overseas:
- Time stationed outside the U.S. still counts as living in the U.S. for EITC purposes
- Your children can meet the residency test even if stationed abroad
- Keep records of your assignment orders

Disability and EITC

Receiving Disability Payments:
Long-term disability benefits received before minimum retirement age COUNT as earned income for EITC if:
- You haven't reached minimum retirement age (defined by your employer's plan)
- The payments are from an employer-paid insurance policy

Disability benefits that DON'T count as earned income:
- Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI)
- Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
- VA disability benefits
- Workers' compensation

Disabled Children:
- A permanently and totally disabled child of ANY age can be your qualifying child
- "Permanently and totally disabled" means:
  - Unable to engage in any substantial gainful activity
  - Condition expected to last continuously for at least 12 months or result in death
- You must be able to provide a doctor's certification if requested

Self-Employment and EITC

Calculating Self-Employment Earned Income:
1. Start with net profit from Schedule C or Schedule F
2. Subtract one-half of self-employment tax
3. Result is your earned income from self-employment

Special Self-Employment Situations:

Ministers and Religious Workers:
- Income reported on Form W-2 (box 1) counts as earned income
- Housing allowance is NOT earned income for EITC
- Self-employment earnings from ministerial services count

Statutory Employees:
- Check box 13 on Form W-2
- Report income on Schedule C
- Counts as self-employment income

Farm Income:
- Use Schedule F
- Net farm profit or loss affects earned income
- Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) payments can be elected to count as earned income

Business Losses:
- If you have a loss, it reduces your total earned income
- You cannot have negative earned income
- If loss exceeds other earned income, earned income is zero

Students and EITC

Full-Time Students:
- If YOU are a full-time student, you can still claim EITC if you otherwise qualify
- If your CHILD is a full-time student, they may qualify until age 24
- The student age test is different for taxpayer vs. qualifying child

What Counts as a Student:
- Enrolled for the number of hours/courses considered full-time
- At least 5 months during the year
- At a school with regular teaching staff and curriculum
- Includes colleges, universities, technical schools, trade schools

Work-Study Programs:
- Income from work-study counts as earned income
- Scholarship/grant money generally does NOT count

Separated or Divorced Parents

Who Claims the Child:
- Generally, the custodial parent (who the child lived with for more nights)
- Custodial parent can release the claim using Form 8332
- But Form 8332 only releases dependency exemption and child tax credit, NOT EITC
- For EITC, the child must meet the residency test (lived with you more than 6 months)

Tiebreaker Rules:
If both parents could claim the child:
1. The parent with whom the child lived longer can claim EITC
2. If equal time, the parent with higher AGI can claim EITC
3. If one parent but the other doesn't claim, a non-parent relative with higher AGI might claim

Important: The rules for child tax credit and EITC are different!

Foster Parents and EITC

Foster Children Can Be Qualifying Children If:
- Placed by an authorized placement agency
- Placed by court order
- Child meets all four tests (Relationship, Age, Residency, Joint Return)
- Must have lived with you for more than half the year

Foster Care Payments:
- Difficulty of care payments from state/agency are NOT taxable income
- They also don't count as earned income
- You must have OTHER earned income to claim EITC
- Keep records showing authorized placement

Adoption and EITC

Adopted Children:
- Treated the same as biological children for EITC
- Includes legally adopted children and children placed for adoption
- Must meet all four qualifying child tests

Adoption Assistance Payments:
- Generally not taxable if for qualified adoption expenses
- Don't count as earned income
- You need other earned income to claim EITC

International Adoptions:
- Child must have valid SSN
- Until finalized, may be treated as placed for adoption

Native American/Tribal Issues

Tribal Income:
- Per capita payments from tribal land or natural resources may be excluded from income
- If excluded, they don't count as earned income for EITC
- Check specific tribal agreements and IRS guidance

Reservations:
- Must live in the U.S. for residency test
- Tribal land within the U.S. counts
- Keep documentation of residence

Incarceration

Taxpayers in Prison:
- You cannot claim EITC for any month you were incarcerated
- Even one day in a month makes that month ineligible
- Upon release, you can claim EITC for months not incarcerated if you otherwise qualify

Children of Incarcerated Parents:
- Child can still be your qualifying child if they meet the tests
- Temporary absence (incarceration) counts as living with you if:
  - The absence is temporary
  - You maintain the home
  - Child returns after release

Homeless Individuals and EITC

No Permanent Address:
- You can still claim EITC
- Shelter addresses can be used
- Temporary addresses are acceptable
- Child must have lived with you for more than half the year

Documentation:
- School records showing same address
- Shelter records
- Letters from social service agencies
- Any evidence showing child lived with you

Immigrant and Non-Citizen Issues

Valid Social Security Numbers Required:
- You must have an SSN valid for employment
- Spouse must have an SSN valid for employment (if filing jointly)
- Children must have SSNs valid for employment
- ITINs (Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers) do NOT qualify for EITC

Resident Aliens:
- Must be U.S. resident alien for entire year
- Use the Substantial Presence Test or Green Card Test
- Nonresident aliens cannot claim EITC

Death of Spouse or Child

Deceased Spouse:
- If spouse died during the year, you may be able to file jointly for that year
- You may qualify as a qualifying surviving spouse in following years
- This affects your income limits and filing status

Deceased Child:
- A child who died during the year can be your qualifying child
- Child must have lived with you for more than half the time they were alive
- You need proof of birth and death

Amending Returns for Missed EITC

You Can Go Back 3 Years:
- If you didn't claim EITC but qualified, file Form 1040-X (Amended Return)
- You have 3 years from the original return due date
- You can still get refunds for those years

How to Amend:
- Complete Form 1040-X
- Attach Schedule EIC if you have qualifying children
- Include any supporting documentation
- Explain why you're amending

COVID-19 Special Rules (If Applicable)

Looking Backward Option:
- For tax years affected by COVID, special rules allowed using prior year income
- Check if any disaster-related special rules apply to your situation
- Economic Impact Payments did NOT count as income

Temporary Work Disruptions:
- Unemployment doesn't count as earned income
- But temporary absence from work didn't affect qualifying child residency test

Remember: Each situation is unique. When in doubt, consult IRS Publication 596 or a qualified tax professional.

Source: IRS Publication 596, IRS Publication 501, IRS Publication 519, Various IRS Notices

title: Eitc Audit And Documentation
content:
EITC Audits, Documentation, and Compliance

Understanding EITC Audits and What to Expect

The EITC has higher audit rates than many other tax credits due to its complexity and history of errors. However, if you're honest and have proper documentation, an audit doesn't need to be stressful.

Why EITC Returns Are Audited

Common Reasons for EITC Audits:
1. Qualifying child issues - child claimed by multiple people, child doesn't meet tests
2. Income discrepancies - reported income doesn't match IRS records
3. Filing status questions - particularly Head of Household claims
4. Self-employment income concerns - unusually high expenses or losses
5. Prior year issues - previously disallowed EITC claims
6. Random selection - some returns are randomly selected for audit

Red Flags That May Trigger an Audit:
- Claiming children who don't have valid SSNs
- Same child claimed by multiple tax preparers or taxpayers
- Income amounts that seem inconsistent with prior years
- Rounded numbers suggesting estimates rather than actual figures
- Pattern of claiming EITC every year with borderline income
- Using a tax preparer with history of fraudulent claims

Types of EITC Audits

1. CORRESPONDENCE AUDIT (Most Common):
- Conducted entirely by mail
- IRS sends Letter 566 or similar notice
- Requests specific documentation
- You respond by mail with required documents
- Usually resolved within 30-90 days

2. OFFICE AUDIT:
- You visit an IRS office
- Bring requested documents
- Meet with IRS auditor
- Usually scheduled in advance
- Less common for EITC

3. FIELD AUDIT:
- IRS agent visits your home or business
- Rare for EITC-only issues
- Usually involves other tax issues too

Documents You Should Keep

ALWAYS Keep for at Least 3 Years:

For Qualifying Children:
1. Birth certificates or adoption papers
2. School records (showing child's name, dates, and your address)
3. Medical records (showing your address and child's name)
4. Childcare provider records
5. Form 8332 (if applicable for divorced/separated parents)
6. Court documents for custody arrangements
7. Any official document showing child lived with you

For Income:
1. All Forms W-2
2. Forms 1099 (all types)
3. Business records if self-employed (receipts, invoices, bank statements)
4. Schedule C with all supporting documentation
5. Bank statements showing income deposits
6. Pay stubs for the entire year

For Filing Status:
1. Documents showing marital status
2. Proof of household expenses paid
3. Utility bills in your name
4. Rent receipts or mortgage statements
5. Grocery receipts and household expense records

General Records:
1. Copy of filed tax return
2. All IRS correspondence
3. Proof of address throughout the year
4. Any relevant court orders or legal documents

How to Respond to an IRS EITC Audit

STEP 1: Don't Panic
- An audit letter doesn't mean you did something wrong
- It's a verification process
- Respond calmly and thoroughly

STEP 2: Read the Letter Carefully
- Note the specific items being questioned
- Check the response deadline (usually 30 days)
- Understand exactly what documentation is needed

STEP 3: Gather Your Documentation
- Collect all documents listed in the IRS letter
- Make copies - never send originals unless specifically required
- Organize documents clearly
- Label everything

STEP 4: Prepare Your Response
- Write a cover letter explaining each document
- Be clear and concise
- Address each question or concern
- Provide contact information

STEP 5: Send Your Response
- Use certified mail with return receipt
- Keep copies of everything you send
- Send before the deadline
- If you need more time, contact the IRS immediately

STEP 6: Follow Up
- Check the status of your audit after 30 days
- Respond to any additional requests promptly
- Keep all correspondence

Common Audit Questions and How to Answer

QUESTION: "Prove the child lived with you for more than 6 months"
PROVIDE:
- School records showing your address
- Medical records showing your address
- Childcare provider statement
- Letter from school or doctor
- Utility bills showing your address
- Calendar or diary showing child's presence (if available)

QUESTION: "Prove your relationship to the child"
PROVIDE:
- Birth certificate
- Adoption papers
- Legal guardianship documents
- Foster care placement documents
- Court orders

QUESTION: "Prove the child's age"
PROVIDE:
- Birth certificate
- Passport
- School records showing age/grade
- Medical records showing birthdate

QUESTION: "Prove your filing status"
PROVIDE:
- Marriage certificate or divorce decree
- Records showing you paid more than half household costs
- Bills and receipts in your name
- Bank statements showing payments

QUESTION: "Verify your earned income"
PROVIDE:
- All W-2s
- All 1099s
- Business records if self-employed
- Bank statements
- Contracts or agreements

Form 8862: Information to Claim EITC After Disallowance

If your EITC was reduced or disallowed in a prior year, you may need to file Form 8862 before you can claim EITC again.

You MUST file Form 8862 if:
- Your EITC was reduced or disallowed for any reason other than math/clerical error
- You're now claiming EITC again
- The disallowance was for a tax year after 1996

You DON'T need Form 8862 if:
- You didn't claim EITC in the intervening years
- The only reason for disallowance was math or clerical error
- You've already filed Form 8862 and been approved

EITC Ban Periods

Serious Violations Lead to Ban:

2-Year Ban:
- Reckless or intentional disregard of EITC rules
- Cannot claim EITC for 2 years

10-Year Ban:
- Fraudulent EITC claim
- Cannot claim EITC for 10 years

Lifetime Ban:
- Conviction of fraud in claiming EITC
- Can NEVER claim EITC again

During the ban:
- You cannot claim EITC even if you otherwise qualify
- The ban applies even if your circumstances change
- No exceptions

How to Avoid a Ban:
- Be honest on your tax return
- Only claim children who meet ALL tests
- Report all income accurately
- Keep proper documentation
- Don't exaggerate expenses or losses
- Use reputable tax preparers

EITC Due Diligence for Tax Preparers

If you use a tax preparer, they must:
- Complete Form 8867 (Paid Preparer's Due Diligence Checklist)
- Ask appropriate questions about your EITC claim
- Review your documents
- Keep records of their due diligence
- Not make fraudulent claims

Your Responsibilities:
- Provide truthful information
- Give preparer all necessary documents
- Review your return before signing
- Understand what's on your return
- You're ultimately responsible for your return's accuracy

Identity Theft and EITC

If Someone Files Using Your Information:
1. File Form 14039 (Identity Theft Affidavit)
2. File your legitimate return on paper
3. Contact IRS Identity Protection Specialized Unit
4. Keep records of all actions taken
5. Monitor your IRS account

IRS May:
- Issue you an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN)
- Flag your account for extra security
- Require additional verification for future returns

Preventing EITC Fraud

Protect Yourself:
1. Guard your SSN and your children's SSNs
2. Choose tax preparers carefully
3. Review your return thoroughly before signing
4. File early to prevent fraudulent returns
5. Use IRS e-file
6. Monitor "Where's My Refund?" for unauthorized filings
7. Check your IRS transcript periodically

Warning Signs of Preparer Fraud:
- Promises specific refund amounts before seeing documents
- Charges fees based on refund percentage
- Suggests claiming ineligible children
- Wants refund direct deposited to their account
- Won't sign return or provide PTIN
- Won't give you a copy of your return

What to Do If You Made a Mistake

If You Realize You Made an Error:
1. File an amended return (Form 1040-X) as soon as possible
2. Pay back any excess credit received
3. Include an explanation
4. This shows good faith and may prevent penalties

Voluntary Disclosure:
- Better to admit an error than wait for audit
- IRS looks favorably on voluntary corrections
- May reduce or eliminate penalties

Getting Help

Free Resources:
- IRS EITC Assistant Tool (online)
- IRS Publication 596
- Local IRS Taxpayer Assistance Centers
- IRS phone helpline: 1-800-829-1040

Free Tax Preparation:
- VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) for income under $60,000
- TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly) age 60+
- IRS Free File for income under $73,000

Professional Help:
- Enrolled Agents (EAs)
- Certified Public Accountants (CPAs)
- Tax Attorneys
- IRS-certified preparers

If You Can't Pay:
- IRS offers payment plans
- Request installment agreement
- May qualify for penalty abatement
- Don't ignore the issue

Important Rights

As a Taxpayer, You Have the Right To:
1. Quality service from the IRS
2. Be informed about tax laws
3. Pay only the correct amount of tax
4. Challenge the IRS's position
5. Appeal an IRS decision
6. Finality (limits on audit periods)
7. Privacy and confidentiality
8. Professional and courteous treatment
9. Representation (can hire someone to represent you)
10. A fair and just tax system

Taxpayer Advocate Service:
- Independent organization within IRS
- Helps if you're experiencing hardship
- Free assistance
- Can intervene on your behalf
- Call 1-877-777-4778

Final Tips for EITC Compliance

1. Keep organized records from the beginning of the year
2. Use IRS EITC Assistant before filing
3. Double-check all SSNs and dates
4. Be honest - never exaggerate or lie
5. Respond promptly to all IRS correspondence
6. Keep copies of everything for at least 3 years
7. Use reputable tax preparation services
8. File electronically when possible
9. Read your return carefully before signing
10. When in doubt, ask for professional help

Remember: The EITC exists to help working families. If you legitimately qualify and have proper documentation, you have nothing to fear from an audit.

Source: IRS Publication 596, IRS Circular 230, Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, IRS Audit Process Guidelines

title: Irs Official Qualifying Child Rules
content:
IRS Official Qualifying Child Rules for EITC
Source: IRS.gov Official Website

A child is a qualifying child for EITC if they meet ALL 4 of these tests:

TEST 1: AGE REQUIREMENT

To be a qualifying child for the EITC, your child must be:

Option A: Any age and permanently and totally disabled at any time during the year.
- The child can be of any age if they are permanently and totally disabled
- For more information, see IRS guidelines on Disability and Earned Income Tax Credit

Option B: Under age 19 at the end of the year and younger than you (or your spouse, if you file a joint return)
- Must be younger than you or your spouse
- Age is determined as of December 31 of the tax year

Option C: Under age 24 at the end of the year and a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and younger than you (or your spouse, if you file a joint return)
- Must be a full-time student
- Must attend for at least 5 months during the year
- Must be younger than you or your spouse

FULL-TIME STUDENT DEFINITION:
To be considered full-time, the student must have enrolled for the number of hours or courses their school considers to be full-time attendance. Students who work on "co-op" jobs in private industry as a part of a school's official program are also considered full-time students.

SCHOOL DEFINITION:
For the EITC, a school IS:
- Elementary school
- Junior or senior high school
- College or university
- Technical, trade or mechanical school

A school is NOT:
- On-the-job training course
- Correspondence school
- School offering courses only through the Internet

TEST 2: RELATIONSHIP REQUIREMENT

To be a qualifying child for the EITC, your child must be your:
- Son, daughter, stepchild, adopted child or foster child
- Brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, stepsister or stepbrother
- Grandchild, niece or nephew

ADOPTED CHILD DEFINITION:
An adopted child is a child who is lawfully placed with you for legal adoption.

FOSTER CHILD DEFINITION:
For the EITC, you can only claim a foster child that is placed with you by:
- A State or local government agency
- An Indian tribal government
- A tax-exempt organization licensed by a state or an Indian tribal government
- A court order

TEST 3: RESIDENCY REQUIREMENT

To be a qualifying child for the EITC, your child must live in the same home as you in the United States for more than half of the tax year.

The United States includes:
- The 50 states
- The District of Columbia
- U.S. military bases

The United States does NOT include:
- United States possessions such as Guam, the Virgin Islands or Puerto Rico

BIRTH OR DEATH OF A CHILD:
If the child was born or died during year for which you claim the EITC and they lived with you for more than half of their life during that year, we consider that more than half of the year for the EITC.

TEMPORARY TIME AWAY FROM HOME:
If your child was temporarily away from home, we count that as time lived with you. 

Temporary absences include:
- Illness or hospitalization
- School attendance, vacation, business or military service
- Detention in a juvenile facility
- Kidnapping

SPECIAL RESIDENCY SITUATIONS:
- Homeless shelters count as living with you
- Military personnel stationed outside the United States still meet the residency requirement
- Extended active duty situations may have special rules
- Kidnapped children may meet special rules

TEST 4: JOINT RETURN REQUIREMENT

To be a qualifying child for the EITC, your child must not have filed a joint return with another person (for example, their husband or wife) to claim any credits such as the EITC.

EXCEPTION:
Your child CAN file a joint tax return only to get a tax refund on tax withheld from their paycheck. If they file only to claim a refund and neither spouse would owe tax if filing separately, this exception applies.

TIEBREAKER RULES - ONLY ONE PERSON MAY CLAIM A QUALIFYING CHILD

A child may meet all the requirements and qualify more than one person for the following child-related benefits:
- Dependency exemption
- EITC
- Child tax credit/credit for other dependents/additional child tax credit
- Head of household filing status, or
- Dependent care credit/exclusion for dependent care benefits

However, even if two or more persons have the same qualifying child, only one person can claim the child as a qualifying child for all these benefits.

TIEBREAKER RULES WHEN TWO OR MORE PERSONS CAN CLAIM THE SAME CHILD:

Rule 1: If only one of the persons is the child's parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent.

Rule 2: If the parents file a joint return together and can claim the child as a qualifying child, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parents.

Rule 3: If the parents don't file a joint return together but both parents claim the child as a qualifying child, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent with whom the child lived for the longer period in the tax year.

Rule 4: If the child lived with each parent for the same amount of time, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent who had the higher adjusted gross income (AGI) for the tax year.

Rule 5: If no parent can claim the child as a qualifying child, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the person who had the highest AGI for the tax year.

Rule 6: If a parent can claim the child as a qualifying child but no parent does so claim the child, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the person who had the highest AGI for the tax year, but only if that person's AGI is higher than the highest AGI of any parent of the child who can claim the child.

IMPORTANT NOTE ABOUT TIEBREAKER RULES:
Special rules apply for parents who are divorced, separated, or who are living apart. If you can't claim the qualifying child because of the tiebreaker rules, you may be eligible to claim the EITC with no qualifying child.

PROOF OF QUALIFICATION

If you are audited after claiming the Earned Income Credit, you will need to provide documents proving that your child qualifies.

Documents you may need to provide:
- Birth certificates or adoption records (for relationship test)
- School records showing name, address, and dates (for age and residency tests)
- Medical records showing name and address (for residency test)
- Childcare provider records (for residency test)
- Any official documents showing the child lived with you

Use the IRS Form 886-H-EIC Toolkit to find the specific documents you need to send to prove you can claim the EITC with a qualifying child.

OTHER CREDITS YOU MAY QUALIFY FOR

If you qualify for the EITC, you may also qualify for other tax credits:
- Child tax credit and the credit for other dependents
- Child and Dependent Care Credit
- Education Credits (American Opportunity Tax Credit and Lifetime Learning Credit)

These credits have their own rules and requirements. Meeting the EITC qualifying child tests doesn't automatically qualify you for these other credits, but it's a good indicator you should check them out.

SUMMARY CHECKLIST FOR QUALIFYING CHILD

Your child must meet ALL FOUR tests:
☐ AGE: Under 19 (or under 24 if student, or any age if disabled) and younger than you
☐ RELATIONSHIP: Your son, daughter, sibling, or descendant of these
☐ RESIDENCY: Lived with you in the U.S. for more than half the year
☐ JOINT RETURN: Did not file a joint return to claim credits

If all four boxes can be checked, the child qualifies for EITC purposes.

For complete official information, see:
- IRS Publication 596, Earned Income Credit (EIC)
- IRS Publication 501, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information
- IRS.gov EITC Assistant tool

Source: IRS.gov official website, IRS Publication 596
Last Updated: 2024

title: Eitc Common Mistakes
content:
Common EITC Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Top EITC Errors and Prevention Strategies

MISTAKE #1: Filing Status Errors
Error: Filing as "Married Filing Separately"
- If you're married, you generally cannot claim EITC if you file separately
Exception: You may be able to claim if you meet specific requirements for being "considered unmarried"

How to Avoid:
- If you're married, file jointly to claim EITC
- If separated, check if you meet the requirements to be "considered unmarried"
- Consult IRS Pub 596 Table 2 for your specific situation

MISTAKE #2: Social Security Number Issues
Common Errors:
- Using an ITIN instead of SSN
- SSN not valid for employment
- Expired or missing SSN for qualifying children
- Wrong SSN on tax return

How to Avoid:
- Ensure all SSNs are valid and issued before the tax return due date
- SSNs must be issued by the Social Security Administration (not ITINs)
- Double-check all numbers before filing
- Apply for SSNs well before tax season

MISTAKE #3: Qualifying Child Errors
Common Errors:
- Child doesn't meet all four tests (Relationship, Age, Residency, Joint Return)
- Child didn't live with you for more than 6 months
- Child is over age limits
- Claiming the same child as someone else

How to Avoid:
- Use the IRS EITC Assistant tool online
- Keep detailed records of where your child lived
- Understand the age limits: under 19, or under 24 if full-time student
- Communicate with other family members about who will claim each child
- Use Form 8332 for divorced/separated parents

MISTAKE #4: Income Calculation Errors
Common Errors:
- Including non-earned income as earned income
- Exceeding the investment income limit ($11,000 for 2024)
- Not reporting all income sources
- Incorrectly calculating self-employment income

How to Avoid:
- Only count wages, salaries, tips, and net self-employment income
- Track all investment income separately
- Report ALL income, even if you don't receive a Form 1099 or W-2
- Use Schedule C to properly calculate self-employment income
- Keep excellent business records if self-employed

MISTAKE #5: Ignoring Income Limits
Error: Earning too much to qualify but still claiming EITC
2024 Income Limits (Married Filing Jointly):
- No qualifying children: $24,210
- 1 qualifying child: $55,768
- 2 qualifying children: $62,449
- 3+ qualifying children: $66,819

How to Avoid:
- Check current year income limits before claiming
- Use IRS EITC Assistant to verify eligibility
- Income limits change annually - don't assume you qualify just because you did last year

MISTAKE #6: Not Claiming EITC When Eligible
Why People Miss Out:
- Don't realize they qualify
- Think they don't need to file a return
- Fear of IRS audit
- Complexity of tax rules

How to Fix:
- File a return even if you're not required to
- You can claim EITC for up to 3 prior years by filing amended returns
- Use free tax preparation services (VITA, TCE)
- The IRS wants you to claim credits you're entitled to!

MISTAKE #7: Incorrect Filing Status Claims
Error: Claiming Head of Household incorrectly
To qualify as Head of Household:
- You must be unmarried or considered unmarried
- You paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home
- A qualifying person lived with you for more than half the year

How to Avoid:
- Understand the specific tests for Head of Household
- Keep records of household expenses
- Don't assume you qualify just because you have children

MISTAKE #8: Missing Schedule EIC
Error: Claiming EITC with qualifying children but not attaching Schedule EIC
- If you have qualifying children, you MUST complete and attach Schedule EIC
- Without it, the IRS will reject your EITC claim

How to Avoid:
- Always complete Schedule EIC if you have qualifying children
- Include all required information for each child
- Tax software usually prompts for this automatically

MISTAKE #9: Not Responding to IRS Notices
Error: Ignoring IRS letters about EITC verification
- The IRS may ask you to prove eligibility
- Not responding = denied claim

How to Avoid:
- Always respond to IRS notices within the deadline
- Keep documentation ready: birth certificates, school records, medical records
- Use certified mail when sending documents to the IRS
- Keep copies of everything you send

MISTAKE #10: Fraudulent Claims
Serious Errors:
- Making up qualifying children
- Falsifying income amounts
- Using fake documents
- Claiming children who don't exist

Consequences:
- Banned from claiming EITC for 2-10 years
- Required to pay back ALL incorrectly claimed credits
- Possible criminal prosecution
- Penalties and interest

How to Avoid:
- Only claim what you're legitimately entitled to
- Be honest on your tax return
- Don't let anyone convince you to lie on your return
- Choose your tax preparer carefully - you're responsible for what's on your return

MISTAKE #11: Not Keeping Records
Error: Unable to prove eligibility if audited
Required Records:
- Birth certificates or other proof of relationship
- School records showing dates and address
- Medical records showing address
- Childcare provider records
- Any official document showing child's address and your address match

How to Avoid:
- Keep records for at least 3 years after filing
- Organize documents by tax year
- Make digital copies as backup
- Keep records showing where children lived throughout the year

MISTAKE #12: Relying on Disreputable Tax Preparers
Warning Signs of Bad Preparers:
- Promise large refunds before looking at your records
- Base fees on percentage of refund
- Don't sign returns they prepare
- Don't provide PTIN (Preparer Tax Identification Number)
- Suggest claiming children who don't qualify

How to Avoid:
- Use IRS-certified preparers
- Check preparer credentials
- Use free services if eligible (VITA, TCE)
- Understand your own return before signing
- Report suspected fraud to the IRS

TIPS FOR SUCCESS

1. Use the IRS EITC Assistant tool before filing
2. Keep organized records throughout the year
3. File electronically for faster processing
4. Consider direct deposit for faster refunds
5. Use reputable tax preparation services
6. Review your return carefully before filing
7. Respond promptly to any IRS correspondence
8. Claim prior year credits if you missed them (within 3 years)
9. Stay informed about annual changes to EITC rules
10. When in doubt, consult a qualified tax professional

Remember: The EITC is a valuable credit worth claiming correctly. Taking time to understand the rules and avoid common mistakes ensures you get the credit you deserve without problems later.

Source: IRS Publication 596, IRS EITC Central, Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration Reports

title: Irs Official Common Errors
content:
IRS Official Guide: Common Errors for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
Source: IRS.gov Official Website

FIVE COMMON ERRORS YOU NEED TO AVOID

The IRS has identified the most common errors that taxpayers make when claiming the Earned Income Tax Credit. Avoiding these errors will help you get your refund faster and reduce the chance of an audit.

ERROR #1: YOUR CHILD DOESN'T QUALIFY

Most EITC errors happen because the child claimed doesn't meet the qualification rules. Your child must meet ALL FOUR tests:

1. RELATIONSHIP TEST: The child must be related to you
   - Your son, daughter, stepchild, adopted child, or foster child
   - Your brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, stepbrother, or stepsister
   - Your grandchild, niece, or nephew

2. RESIDENCY TEST: The child must live in the same home as you for more than half the tax year
   - Must be in the United States (50 states, DC, or U.S. military bases)
   - Temporary absences (school, vacation, medical) count as living with you
   - Must be more than 6 months (183 days)

3. AGE TEST: The child must meet the age requirements
   - Under 19 at end of year and younger than you, OR
   - Under 24 at end of year, a full-time student, and younger than you, OR
   - Any age if permanently and totally disabled

4. JOINT RETURN TEST: The child must not file a joint return with another person
   - Exception: Joint return filed only to claim refund of withheld taxes
   - If filing joint return to claim credits like EITC, child doesn't qualify

HOW TO AVOID THIS ERROR:
✓ Verify all four tests are met
✓ Keep documentation for each test
✓ Use the IRS EITC Assistant to check eligibility
✓ Review the official qualifying child rules on IRS.gov

Related Resource: IRS Publication 596, Qualifying Children for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

ERROR #2: MORE THAN ONE PERSON CLAIMED THE CHILD

This error occurs when multiple people try to claim the same child. Only ONE person can claim a child for EITC purposes.

COMMON SCENARIOS:
- Divorced or separated parents both claiming the same child
- Grandparent and parent both claiming the same child
- Two relatives in the same household both claiming the same child
- Child living with different people during the year

THE RULE:
The child must have lived with you for more than half of the tax year to be YOUR qualifying child.

TIEBREAKER RULES:
If more than one person can claim the same child, the IRS uses tiebreaker rules:
1. Parent has priority over non-parent
2. If both parents claim, child goes to parent child lived with longest
3. If equal time with both parents, child goes to parent with higher AGI
4. If no parent claims, child goes to person with highest AGI

IMPORTANT NOTE FOR DIVORCED/SEPARATED PARENTS:
- Form 8332 releases the dependency exemption and child tax credit
- Form 8332 does NOT release the EITC
- For EITC, the custodial parent (where child lived longest) claims the credit
- Custody agreements don't override IRS rules

HOW TO AVOID THIS ERROR:
✓ Communicate with other potential claimants
✓ Understand tiebreaker rules
✓ Keep records of where child lived throughout the year
✓ Know the difference between dependency exemption and EITC rules
✓ File early to establish your claim

Related Resource: IRS Publication 596, Qualifying Children for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

ERROR #3: SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER OR LAST NAME DON'T MATCH

This is a very common error that's easy to prevent.

THE REQUIREMENT:
The Social Security number and name must match EXACTLY how they appear on the Social Security card for everyone listed on your tax return.

COMMON MISTAKES:
- Transposed digits in SSN
- Wrong SSN entered
- Name doesn't match Social Security card exactly
- Using maiden name when SSN card has married name
- Nicknames instead of legal names
- Misspellings
- Missing hyphens or spaces in names

SPECIAL SITUATIONS:
- Recently married and changed name: Get new Social Security card BEFORE filing
- Recently changed name for any reason: Update with Social Security Administration first
- Child's name doesn't match card: Get corrected card before filing
- Using "Not valid for employment" SSN: These DO NOT qualify for EITC

HOW TO AVOID THIS ERROR:
✓ Have Social Security cards in front of you when preparing return
✓ Double-check every digit of every SSN
✓ Use exact name as it appears on Social Security card
✓ Update Social Security Administration BEFORE filing taxes if name changed
✓ Ensure all SSNs are valid for employment
✓ Don't use ITINs - EITC requires SSNs

WHAT TO DO IF NAMES DON'T MATCH:
1. Contact Social Security Administration
2. Update name on Social Security card
3. Wait to file tax return until new card received
4. Use exact name from new card on tax return

Related Resource: IRS Publication 596, Qualifying Children for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

ERROR #4: MARRIED AND FILED AS SINGLE OR HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD

Using the wrong filing status is a serious error that can disqualify your EITC claim entirely.

THE RULE:
You can't claim the EITC using the single or head of household filing status if you are married AND you lived with your spouse during the last six months of the year.

COMMON SCENARIOS THAT CAUSE THIS ERROR:
- Married taxpayers filing as Single when they should file Married Filing Jointly
- Married taxpayers filing as Head of Household incorrectly
- Not understanding "considered unmarried" rules
- Temporary separations treated as permanent
- Living apart but not legally separated

CORRECT FILING STATUSES:
If you're married and lived together any time in last 6 months of the year:
- You MUST file as Married Filing Jointly or Married Filing Separately
- You generally CANNOT claim EITC if filing Married Filing Separately
- Therefore, if married and living together, you must file jointly to claim EITC

EXCEPTION - "CONSIDERED UNMARRIED":
You may be able to file as Head of Household and claim EITC even if married if:
- You file a separate return from your spouse
- You paid more than half the cost of keeping up your home for the year
- Your spouse did not live in your home during the last 6 months of the year
- Your home was the main home of your child, stepchild, or foster child for more than half the year
- You can claim the child as a dependent

HOW TO AVOID THIS ERROR:
✓ Know your true marital status on December 31
✓ Understand "considered unmarried" rules
✓ Don't file as Single if you're married
✓ Use IRS Interactive Tax Assistant to determine correct filing status
✓ Keep records if claiming "considered unmarried" status
✓ Consult a tax professional if your situation is complex

Related Resource: IRS Publication 501, Who Qualifies for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

ERROR #5: OVER OR UNDERREPORTING YOUR INCOME OR EXPENSES

Accurate income and expense reporting is critical for EITC. The IRS receives copies of all your income documents and will catch discrepancies.

INCOME REPORTING REQUIREMENTS:
Include ALL forms of income when calculating your earned income:
- Forms W-2 (all of them if you had multiple jobs)
- Forms W-2G (gambling winnings)
- Forms 1099-MISC (miscellaneous income)
- Forms 1099-NEC (non-employee compensation)
- Forms 1099-K (payment card and third party network transactions)
- All other records of income, including income not reported on an IRS form
- Cash payments
- Tips not reported on W-2
- Self-employment income

IF INCOME DOESN'T MATCH IRS RECORDS:
You may be required to submit additional documentation such as:
- Periodic pay statements (pay stubs)
- Electronic payment records
- Bank statements
- A letter from your employer on company letterhead stating:
  * Dates of employment
  * Gross amount of wages paid
  * Withholdings deducted

SELF-EMPLOYMENT INCOME AND EXPENSES:
- Report ALL income you earn from running or owning a business or farm
- You can deduct all ALLOWABLE expenses
- You cannot deduct personal expenses
- You cannot inflate expenses
- Keep detailed records and receipts

COMMON MISTAKES:
- Forgetting to report a W-2 from a short-term job
- Not reporting cash income
- Overstating business expenses
- Deducting personal expenses as business expenses
- Not keeping receipts for business expenses
- Underreporting income to stay under EITC limits
- Including non-earned income in earned income calculation

HOW TO AVOID THIS ERROR:
✓ Gather ALL income documents before filing
✓ Wait to file until you have all W-2s and 1099s (usually by February)
✓ Report cash and informal income
✓ Keep detailed business records and receipts
✓ Only deduct legitimate business expenses
✓ Don't inflate expenses or reduce income to qualify for more EITC
✓ Use tax software that imports W-2 and 1099 data
✓ Double-check all numbers before filing

CONSEQUENCES OF MISREPORTING:
- Delayed refund while IRS verifies information
- Additional documentation requests
- Denial of EITC claim
- Requirement to pay back incorrectly claimed credit
- Penalties and interest
- Potential EITC ban (2 years, 10 years, or lifetime depending on severity)
- Criminal prosecution in cases of fraud

BE HONEST:
The EITC is valuable, but it's never worth committing fraud. If you honestly report all income and expenses and genuinely qualify, you have nothing to worry about. If you don't qualify, don't try to manipulate numbers to qualify.

ADDITIONAL TIPS TO AVOID ERRORS

1. USE IRS FREE FILE OR TAX SOFTWARE
   - Helps catch common errors
   - Imports income information
   - Checks math automatically
   - Prompts for required forms

2. USE IRS EITC ASSISTANT
   - Free tool on IRS.gov
   - Checks eligibility before filing
   - Estimates credit amount
   - Available in English and Spanish

3. GET FREE TAX HELP
   - VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) for income under $60,000
   - TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly) for age 60+
   - IRS Taxpayer Assistance Centers
   - IRS helpline: 1-800-829-1040

4. FILE ELECTRONICALLY
   - Reduces errors
   - Faster processing
   - Get refund sooner (after mid-February for EITC)

5. CHOOSE DIRECT DEPOSIT
   - Fastest way to get refund
   - No lost or stolen checks
   - No waiting for mail

6. KEEP GOOD RECORDS
   - Keep copies of all documents
   - Maintain records for at least 3 years
   - Be ready if IRS asks for documentation

7. REVIEW BEFORE FILING
   - Check all names and SSNs
   - Verify all income is included
   - Confirm children meet all four tests
   - Ensure correct filing status
   - Read through entire return

8. RESPOND PROMPTLY TO IRS LETTERS
   - Don't ignore IRS correspondence
   - Provide requested documentation quickly
   - Use certified mail for important documents
   - Keep copies of everything you send

WHERE TO FIND MORE INFORMATION

- IRS.gov/EITC - Main EITC page
- IRS Publication 596 - Earned Income Credit (complete guide)
- IRS EITC Assistant - Online eligibility tool
- IRS Free File - Free tax filing for qualifying taxpayers
- Form 886-H-EIC Toolkit - Audit documentation guide

Remember: Taking time to avoid these common errors will help you get your EITC refund faster and reduce the chance of problems with the IRS.

Source: IRS.gov official website
Publication: Common Errors for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
Last Updated: 2024

Disclaimer: This information is for general guidance only. Tax laws are complex and change frequently. Consult IRS Publication 596 or a qualified tax professional for your specific situation. Informational only, not tax advice.

title: Irs Official How To Claim
content:
IRS Official Guide: How to Claim the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
Source: IRS.gov Official Website

FORMS YOU NEED TO FILE

To claim the Earned Income Tax Credit, you must file the appropriate tax forms:

FORM 1040 OR FORM 1040-SR (REQUIRED FOR EVERYONE)
- Form 1040: U.S. Individual Income Tax Return
- Form 1040-SR: U.S. Tax Return for Seniors (alternative for those age 65 or older)

You MUST file one of these forms to claim the EITC, even if you don't owe any tax or are not normally required to file.

SCHEDULE EIC (REQUIRED IF YOU HAVE QUALIFYING CHILDREN)
- Schedule EIC (Form 1040 or 1040-SR): Earned Income Credit
- This form is REQUIRED if you are claiming the EITC with one or more qualifying children
- Provides information about each qualifying child
- Must be attached to your Form 1040 or 1040-SR

SCHEDULE EIC IS NOT REQUIRED if:
- You are claiming the EITC without a qualifying child
- However, you still must meet all other EITC requirements

INFORMATION NEEDED FOR SCHEDULE EIC:
For each qualifying child, you must provide:
- Child's name
- Child's Social Security number
- Child's year of birth
- Child's relationship to you
- Number of months child lived with you in the United States
- Whether child qualifies as a qualifying child for the Child Tax Credit

YOUR REFUND - TIMING AND PROCESSING

EITC REFUND DELAY (BY LAW)
If you claim the EITC, your refund may be delayed. This is required by law to prevent fraud.

BY LAW, the IRS cannot issue EITC refunds before mid-February (usually February 15).

This delay applies to your ENTIRE refund, not just the EITC portion. Even if you have other credits or overpayments, the IRS must hold the entire refund until mid-February if you claim EITC.

EXPECTED REFUND TIMELINE:
The IRS expects most EITC refunds to be available in bank accounts or on debit cards by early March (typically by March 3) if you:
- File electronically
- Choose direct deposit
- Have no other issues with your tax return

FACTORS THAT DELAY REFUNDS:
- Errors on your return
- Missing or incorrect Social Security numbers
- Income discrepancies with IRS records
- Filing paper return instead of e-filing
- Choosing check instead of direct deposit
- Claiming child who doesn't meet all tests
- Other issues requiring review

HOW TO TRACK YOUR REFUND:
Use these IRS tools to check refund status:
- "Where's My Refund?" on IRS.gov
- IRS2Go mobile app
- Call IRS automated refund hotline: 1-800-829-1954

You can check refund status 24 hours after e-filing or 4 weeks after mailing paper return.

HOW TO GET YOUR REFUND FASTER

FASTEST METHOD:
1. E-file your return (file electronically)
2. Choose direct deposit
3. File as soon as you have all documents (but refund still won't come until mid-February)
4. Avoid errors by double-checking everything

E-FILE OPTIONS:
- IRS Free File (for qualifying taxpayers) - Completely FREE
- Commercial tax software (TurboTax, H&R Block, etc.)
- Hire a tax preparer who e-files
- File through VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) - FREE

IRS FREE FILE:
- Available for those with adjusted gross income of $73,000 or less
- Completely free federal return
- Some also offer free state returns
- Access at IRS.gov/FreeFile
- Available in English and Spanish

DIRECT DEPOSIT BENEFITS:
- Money goes directly into your bank account
- Faster than waiting for paper check
- No risk of lost or stolen check
- No need to go to bank to deposit
- Can split refund between up to 3 accounts

AVOID COMMON ERRORS:
Review the IRS list of common EITC errors and avoid them:
- Child doesn't meet all four tests
- Multiple people claiming same child
- Names/SSNs don't match Social Security cards
- Wrong filing status
- Income reporting errors

Each error you avoid speeds up your refund processing.

CLAIMING EITC FOR PRIOR YEARS

DID YOU MISS CLAIMING EITC IN A PREVIOUS YEAR?
You have three years to file and claim a refund from the due date of your tax return.

If you were eligible for EITC but didn't claim it, you can still get that money by filing for prior years:

DEADLINES FOR PRIOR YEAR CLAIMS:
- For 2023 EITC: File by April 15, 2027
- For 2022 EITC: File by April 15, 2026
- For 2021 EITC: File by April 15, 2025

HOW TO FILE FOR PRIOR YEARS:

IF YOU DIDN'T FILE A RETURN AT ALL:
1. Get the correct forms for that tax year (prior year Form 1040)
2. Complete the return for that year
3. Include Schedule EIC if you had qualifying children
4. Mail the return to the IRS (address depends on your state)
5. Write the tax year clearly on the return

IF YOU FILED BUT DIDN'T CLAIM EITC:
1. File an amended return using Form 1040-X
2. Complete Schedule EIC if you have qualifying children
3. Attach any supporting documentation
4. Mail to the appropriate IRS address
5. Allow 16-20 weeks for processing

WHERE TO GET PRIOR YEAR FORMS:
- IRS.gov (search for "prior year forms")
- IRS phone line: 1-800-829-3676
- Local IRS office
- Many tax software programs have prior year versions

CHECK ELIGIBILITY FOR PRIOR YEARS:
Use the IRS EITC Qualification Assistant to determine if you were eligible for EITC in prior years. The tool can calculate estimates for past years.

IMPORTANT NOTES ABOUT PRIOR YEAR CLAIMS:
- Income limits and credit amounts change each year
- Rules may have been different in prior years
- You must have met all requirements for that specific tax year
- Keep documentation for prior year claims

TAX HELP AND ASSISTANCE

FREE TAX PREPARATION HELP:

VITA (VOLUNTEER INCOME TAX ASSISTANCE):
- FREE tax preparation
- For those with income under $60,000
- Available in many communities
- Certified volunteers prepare returns
- Find locations: IRS.gov/VITA or call 1-800-906-9887

TCE (TAX COUNSELING FOR THE ELDERLY):
- FREE tax preparation
- For taxpayers age 60 and older
- Specializes in retirement and pension issues
- Find locations: Call 1-888-227-7669

IRS FREE FILE:
- Free online tax preparation software
- For AGI of $73,000 or less
- Available at IRS.gov/FreeFile

HIRING A TAX PROFESSIONAL:
If you choose to hire someone to prepare your return:
- Choose a reputable preparer
- Check their credentials (CPA, EA, or Annual Filing Season Program participant)
- Never sign a blank return
- Make sure they sign the return and provide their PTIN
- Review the return before signing
- Don't let them charge fees based on refund amount
- Don't let them deposit refund into their account

WHAT TO BRING TO YOUR TAX PREPARER:
- Social Security cards for everyone on return
- All Forms W-2 (wage statements)
- All Forms 1099 (interest, dividends, other income)
- Form 1098-E (student loan interest)
- Form 1098-T (tuition statement)
- Receipts for deductible expenses
- Health insurance information (Form 1095-A if applicable)
- Prior year tax return
- Bank account information for direct deposit

IRS RESOURCES:
- IRS.gov/EITC - Main EITC information page
- EITC Assistant - Online eligibility tool
- Publication 596 - Complete EITC guide
- IRS helpline: 1-800-829-1040 (mention EITC)
- IRS2Go app - Mobile access to refund status and tax info

SPECIAL FILING SITUATIONS

MILITARY MEMBERS:
- Special rules for combat pay
- Can elect to include nontaxable combat pay as earned income
- Time stationed overseas counts as living in U.S.
- See IRS military-specific EITC guidance

CLERGY MEMBERS:
- Housing allowances have special rules
- See IRS clergy-specific EITC guidance

DISASTER VICTIMS:
- May be able to use prior year earned income
- Special rules apply after federally declared disasters
- Check IRS disaster relief announcements

SELF-EMPLOYED:
- Use Schedule C to report business income
- Net profit counts as earned income
- Subtract 1/2 of self-employment tax from earned income
- Keep detailed business records

IMPORTANT REMINDERS

✓ File a return even if you don't owe tax
✓ The EITC is refundable - you can get money even if you owe no tax
✓ E-file and use direct deposit for fastest refund
✓ Refunds won't come until mid-February (required by law)
✓ Avoid errors to prevent delays
✓ Keep copies of all documents
✓ Respond promptly to any IRS letters
✓ You can claim EITC for up to 3 prior years
✓ Free help is available

ADDITIONAL CREDITS YOU MAY QUALIFY FOR

If you qualify for the EITC, you may also qualify for:
- Child Tax Credit (CTC)
- Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC)
- Credit for Other Dependents (ODC)
- Child and Dependent Care Credit
- Education Credits (American Opportunity, Lifetime Learning)

Each credit has its own rules. Check IRS.gov or consult a tax professional to see which credits you qualify for.

WHERE TO FIND MORE HELP

- IRS.gov/EITC - Official IRS EITC page
- IRS Publication 596 - Complete EITC guide
- IRS EITC Assistant - Check eligibility online
- IRS Free File - Free tax software
- VITA locations - Free tax preparation
- 1-800-829-1040 - IRS helpline

Remember: Filing your tax return and claiming EITC is your right if you qualify. Take advantage of free resources and don't leave money on the table!

Source: IRS.gov official website
